deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (dated 1847, published posthumously in the Werke, 1876). The red ink is editorial. It replaces Riemann's notation ^x∂^ν_z with ∂_x^ν z, as prepared for the Werke edition. The pencilled 25 is the page number and 74 is a foliation number. Π(a) = Γ(a+1).

(2) End of a sentence begun on p.24. The value ∂_x^ν z is required to satisfy the 'generalized Taylor series'
 z(x+h) = Σ_{n=1}^{∞} h^{ν-n}/Π(ν-n) ∫^{(n)} ∂_x^ν z dx^n + h^ν/Π(ν) ∂_x^ν z + Σ_{n=1}^{∞} h^{ν+n}/Π(ν+n) d^n(∂_x^ν z)/dx^n.
In modern form: z(x+h) = Σ_{n∈Z} h^{ν+n}/Γ(ν+n+1) D^{ν+n} z(x). The n-fold integrals are D^{ν-n} and the n-fold derivatives are D^{ν+n}. Footnote ***) refers to p.26, note 2. There Riemann asks whether his formula gives all solutions, i.e. whether the C-functions are the only ones annihilating this series. He states this is easy for algebraic functions and open in general.

(3) 'Hieraus folgt': put ν = -m (m a positive integer) in the p.24 definition
 ∂^ν z = 1/Π(-ν-1) ∫_k^x (x-t)^{-ν-1} z(t) dt + Σ_{n≥1} K_n x^{-n-ν}/Π(-n-ν).
[Implicit, mine:] By Cauchy's formula, 1/(m-1)! ∫_k^x (x-t)^{m-1} z dt equals the m-fold iterated integral ∫_k^x…∫ z dt^m. The terms with n > m vanish because 1/Π(negative integer) = 0. Hence
 ∂^{-m} z = ∫_k^{x (m)} z dt^m + Σ_{n=1}^{m} K_n x^{m-n}/(m-n)!.
That is, the m-fold integral plus an arbitrary polynomial of degree m-1.

(4) ∂^0 z = z. [Mine:] By the definition for ν ≥ 0, ∂^0 z = d^m/dx^m ∂^{-m} z. The m-th derivative of the m-fold integral is z, and the polynomial of degree m-1 is killed.

(5) ∂^m z = d^m z/dx^m, by the same argument.

(6) Composition law. ∂^μ ∂^ν z = ∂^{ν+μ} z + (complementary function; the symbol after '+' is most likely C_μ). [Mine:] The extra freedom from the outer operation is C_μ = Σ K'_n x^{-n-μ}/Π(-n-μ). The image of C_ν under the power rule, x^{-n-ν} ↦ x^{-n-ν-μ}Π(-n-ν)/Π(-n-ν-μ), lies in C_{ν+μ}. Hence every value of ∂^{ν+μ} z is a value of ∂^μ ∂^ν z. The converse holds iff C_μ ⊂ C_{ν+μ}. This happens if μ is a positive integer, since then all 1/Π(-n-μ) = 0 and C_μ = 0. It also happens if ν = -m is a negative integer, since by the p.24 footnote every C_{λ} is also a C_{λ-m}, so C_μ = C_{(μ+ν)+m} ⊂ C_{μ+ν}. In these cases both expressions are identical.

(7)-(10) 'From the definition follows, c a constant':
(7) ∂^ν(p+q) = ∂^ν p + ∂^ν q.
(8) ∂^ν(cp) = c ∂^ν p.
(9) ∂_{x+c}^ν z = ∂_x^ν z: invariance under translation of the independent variable, with the lower limit shifted along.
(10) ∂_{cx}^ν z = c^{-ν} ∂_x^ν z: homogeneity. Substituting u = cx, s = ct in the RL integral gives I_u^a = c^a I_x^a, so D_u^ν = c^{-ν} D_x^ν.

The last line begins the definition of 'corresponding values' of ∂^ν z and ∂^μ z, those with all constants k, K equal; it is continued on p.26.
errors: Eq. 2 is asserted as a defining condition without any discussion of convergence. The two-sided series converges only under restrictive conditions. For z = x^b with lower limit 0 it reduces to a two-sided binomial series, which converges only for |h| = |x|. Hardy (1945, 'Riemann's form of Taylor's series') analysed its validity. This is a gap, not an algebraic error.
In the third sum of eq. 2 the denominator in the image looks like Π(ν+h). It should be Π(ν+n); this is a slip of the pen, if the reading is right.

Eq. 6 and eqs 9-10 hold only modulo the complementary functions and with suitably adjusted lower limits. The C-functions are powers of x (origin 0), while the integral has lower limit k. So the power rule used implicitly for ∂^μ C_ν is exact only for k = 0, or with corresponding constants. This is the well-known weak point of Riemann's complementary function, criticized by Cayley (1880). Riemann himself tries to handle it on p.26 via 'corresponding values'.
Eq. 9 needs the lower limit k shifted to k+c, and eq. 10 needs it scaled to ck; neither is stated explicitly.

results.what: Generalized (fractional) Taylor series z(x+h)=Σ_{n∈Z} h^{ν+n}/Γ(ν+n+1) D^{ν+n}z(x), used as the defining property of fractional derivatives
results.modern_name: Riemann's generalized Taylor series (fractional Taylor series)

results.what: Fractional integral for ν=-m reduces to m-fold iterated integral plus an arbitrary polynomial of degree m-1; ∂^0 z = z; ∂^m z = z^{(m)}
results.modern_name: Riemann-Liouville integral / Cauchy formula for repeated integration

results.what: Composition law ∂^μ∂^ν z = ∂^{μ+ν}z + C_μ, with equality iff μ is a positive integer or ν a negative integer
results.modern_name: Semigroup/composition rule for Riemann-Liouville operators (D^n D^ν = D^{n+ν}, D^ν I^m = D^{ν-m})
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann/Liouville; modern form in standard texts (Samko-Kilbas-Marichev)

results.what: Linearity, translation invariance and homogeneity D_{cx}^ν = c^{-ν} D_x^ν
results.modern_name: Elementary properties of the Riemann-Liouville operator (scaling property)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is part of Riemann's 1847 student essay on fractional calculus, published in his Collected Works (1876). The generalized Taylor series is already known in the literature as 'Riemann's form of Taylor's series'. The remaining results are routine properties of the Riemann-Liouville operator. Only the editorial notation changes are manuscript-specific.

transcription_corrections: In eq. 6, the term rendered '+ etc.' is most likely '+ C_μ' (Riemann's symbol for the arbitrary complementary functions defined in the p.24 footnote). This is the reading consistent with the stated converse conditions.
In the third sum of eq. 2 the manuscript appears to read Π(ν+h), a slip for Π(ν+n). The transcription silently gives Π(ν+n).
In eq. 3 the integral is the m-fold integral ∫_K^{x (m)} z_{(t)} dt^m with lower limit K (= k), and the complementary sum runs from n=1 to n=m (written Σ_{n=m}^{n=1}).
'genügen muß' after eq. 2 is followed by the footnote mark ***), which points to note 2 on p.26 ('Note auf Seite 26' in the red margin also refers to eq. 3's note).
